Stoclet Palace, Brussels

Josef Hoffmann’s house for Adolphe Stoclet, 1905–1911: flat white stone planes edged with metal mouldings, with interiors by the Wiener Werkstätte and a mosaic frieze by Klimt.

Source
Wikipedia: Stoclet Palace
Creator
Josef Hoffmann; Wiener Werkstätte
Made
1905–1911
Style
Vienna Secession (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Austere, refined, monumental

It shows part of the tower and a window bay, not the whole house. The house is private and closed to visitors, so I saw no interior. No image is stored.

Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Wikipedia: the house was designed by Josef Hoffmann for the financier Adolphe Stoclet and built between 1905 and 1911 in the Vienna Secession style. It was the first residential project of the Wiener Werkstätte. Its features include geometric volumes, symmetry, straight lines, concrete covered with marble plaques, and mosaic friezes by Gustav Klimt. It is still owned by the Stoclet family and not open to visitors. Wikipedia.

Wikipedia: the house has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009. The UNESCO listing is Stoclet House, 1298, which I did not open.

Observed

  • The wall is faced with large flat, pale stone plates with fine joints.
  • Every edge of the wall is outlined by a continuous band of dark metal moulding with a repeated, stepped pattern, so each plane reads as a framed panel.
  • A tall bay holds three narrow windows, each divided into many small square panes by white bars.
  • Three sculpted heads sit in square recesses above the windows, inside the moulding frame.
  • A black metal railing of squares and spirals stands on the roof edge above.

Why it belongs

Outlining every plane with a thin band is the architectural version of the style’s ruled frames on paper. The building has little ornament apart from these edges.

Wikipedia’s Wiener Werkstätte article calls the house a pioneering work of Art Deco; the continuous edge bands point toward that later style.

Borrow

Outline each panel with a thin, patterned or dark band instead of a shadow or a fill change.

Divide a tall narrow element into a column of small squares.
